papers.title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
papers.summary: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
papers.summary: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and R\"ossler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

papers.title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
papers.summary: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

papers.title: Physics-informed and event-aware forecasting of ammonia emissions in aerobic chicken manure composting bioreactors: A PINN-PatchTST-GPR framework with symbolic dynamic extraction
papers.summary: Predicting ammonia (NH3) concentrations during aerobic chicken manure composting provides critical feedforward signals for intelligent aeration. However, the concurrence of long-term biochemical evolution and intermittent forced-aeration pulses poses significant modeling hurdles across steady baselines, transient surges, and risk quantification. Existing data-driven models lack physical consistency, while mechanistic kinetic models struggle with environmental disturbances. To bridge this gap, we propose PINN-PatchTST-GPR, a physics-informed neuro-symbolic forecasting framework. Validated on a 28-day composting campaign across six vertical bioreactors, the framework couples a channel-independent PatchTST backbone with macroscopic kinetic constraints, dynamic physical bounds, and a Gaussian process regression (GPR) event specialist. Multi-channel sensor streams drive discrete differential equation residuals and non-negativity bounds, strictly ensuring physical plausibility. A block-split conformal prediction module yields nominal 90% distribution-free prediction intervals, while PySINDy and PySR extract low-complexity symbolic equations for quiescent and surge regimes. The model achieves an overall RMSE of 0.8256 +/- 0.0132 ppm, R2 of 0.9817 +/- 0.0006, Epeak of 1.6793 +/- 0.0725 ppm, and Etime of 0.7 +/- 0.2 min. For uncertainty quantification, it attains PICP90 of 99.792 +/- 0.047%, MPIW of 6.951 +/- 0.128 ppm, and IS0.1 of 6.968 +/- 0.128 ppm. Symbolically, PySINDy yields an RMSE of 0.4624 +/- 0.0758 ppm (R2 = 0.9896), while PySR yields 2.4084 +/- 0.0864 ppm (R2 = 0.9523). Biologically, the 20-min aeration strategy minimizes cumulative NH3 emissions. Overall, PINN-PatchTST-GPR harmonizes global forecasting, localized transient responsiveness, and risk quantification for precision composting.

papers.title: From Language-Specific to Cross-DSL: Semantic-Role-Guided Model Completion with LLMs
papers.summary: The rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs), trained on vast and diverse corpora, has positioned them as a promising source of domain knowledge to assist modelers. However, leveraging LLMs for model completion remains challenging: suggestions must respect both the syntax of a domain-specific language (DSL) and the intended domain semantics, while remaining consistent with an evolving model. This paper presents RAFiC, an LLM-based approach for iterative domain model completion that generalizes across DSLs. It drives completion using metamodel information to ensure syntactic validity and enriches prompts with semantic-role annotations to better capture the intended modeling role of DSL elements. The approach provides context-aware, incremental guidance during model construction. We evaluate RAFiC through an ablation-based comparative study over three DSLs and two scenarios per DSL to isolate the contribution of syntactic and semantic guidance. Across these six scenarios, semantic role guidance improves contribution rate in every case, and RAFiC improves completion effectiveness over weaker prompting configurations in most of them. The largest gains occur for DSLs that are less represented in LLM training data. In these cases, iterative guidance leads to earlier and more stable accepted suggestions, while semantic role guidance improves their relevance.

papers.title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
papers.summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

papers.title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
papers.summary: Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at https://github.com/Hamza-Kamil/NAP-WAVE.

papers.title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
papers.summary: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker <CHECK> is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.

papers.title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
papers.summary: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.

papers.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
papers.summary: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.

papers.title: Skill-Latent Rewards: LLM-Guided Reward Formulation for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Long-horizon reinforcement learning under sparse and delayed feedback remains an open challenge. Existing return-decomposition methods redistribute episodic rewards to ease credit assignment, but they operate on raw state--action transitions and disregard the subgoal structure that governs meaningful progress in complex tasks. We propose Skill-LR, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework in which a vision--language model identifies the agent's active subgoal at each timestep and a large language model generates a matching latent reward formulation through a two-stage prompting process. By conditioning reward signals on the currently active subgoal, Skill-LR produces stage-specific credit that evolves with the hierarchical plan, reducing temporal variance and improving sample efficiency. On multi-stage MiniGrid and BabyAI benchmarks, including DoorKey and Unlock-to-Unlock, Skill-LR converges faster and more reliably than sparse environmental rewards and strong credit-assignment baselines such as RUDDER and LaRe, demonstrating that subgoal-aligned latent rewards offer a principled path toward stable, interpretable credit assignment in long-horizon tasks.

papers.title: Internal Verdicts Track Evidence: A Template-Controlled Neutrosophic Reading of Epistemic States in Large Language Models via the Jacobian Lens
papers.summary: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.

papers.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Decision Support in Gait Analysis: A Proof-of-Concept
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential for clinical decision support but lack specialized biomechanical knowledge required for accurate gait analysis interpretation. We developed and evaluated a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to enhance LLM-generated clinical explanations for ankle fracture rehabilitation using ground reaction force data. Using the GaitRec dataset (503 subjects: 211 healthy, 292 ankle fracture patients), we implemented a five-stage pipeline integrating: (1) machine learning classification (91.3\% accuracy); (2) Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for explainable feature identification; (3) RAG knowledge base from peer-reviewed biomechanics literature; (4) GPT-5 explanation generation with and without retrieval augmentation; and (5) double-blind evaluation by experienced physical therapists across five clinical criteria. RAG augmentation produced statistically significant improvements in Clini-cal Benefit (mean difference=0.60, p=0.047, {\delta}=0.49) and Completeness (mean difference=0.70, p=0.049, {\delta}=0.49), both demonstrating large effect sizes. Baseline GPT-5 achieved strong performance across all criteria (\textgreater4.0/5.0). This proof-of-concept demonstrates that augmenting general-purpose LLMs with domain-specific knowledge meaningfully enhances actionable, evidence-based clinical guidance---dimensions most critical for rehabilitation decision-making. The framework provides a scalable approach for integrating AI into specialized clinical workflows without costly model retraining.

papers.title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

papers.title: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study
papers.summary: Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed. These findings suggest that target-aligned conjecture generation depends on combining information that identifies relevant objects with information that constrains admissible claims.

papers.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
papers.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

papers.title: Decision 1.0: Towards Open Decision Foundation Models
papers.summary: Intelligent software needs reusable judgments inside its control flow: selecting an action, testing a condition, or assessing evidence against a rubric. We present Decision 1.0, an open-weight family that turns textual state and runtime-defined questions into typed probability distributions. Its Choice, Noul, and Score interface lets applications specify outcomes at inference time and compose predictions into agents and workflows. Each question produces its candidate distribution without autoregressive text generation. Six models cover bidirectional encoder and causal decoder architectures, including a workflow specialist. Training draws on verifiable tasks, natural-language annotations, and workflow adaptation. On a common decision benchmark, Lux-9B achieves 84.17\% on explicit decisions and 91.25\% on inference, with a weighted overall score of 77.22\%. Results also expose gaps in composition, transfer, and probability calibration. Released weights and inference code provide a basis for developing decision models as reusable components of software.

papers.title: ReVision: Selective Intrinsic Reasoning for Tool-Augmented, Reasoning-Intensive VQA
papers.summary: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

papers.title: GRAFT: Cross-Backbone LoRA Reuse for Continual Language and Multimodal Learning
papers.summary: In continual learning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to acquire new capabilities through lightweight adapters such as LoRA, yet the reuse of pretrained adapters is typically restricted to models sharing the same backbone. This limits the transfer of learned capabilities from language models to multimodal models. We propose GRAFT (Generalist Reuse of Adapters via Feature-space Transfer), a framework for cross-backbone LoRA reuse. GRAFT retrieves the most relevant pretrained LoRA adapter from a modality-aware library and maps it into the target backbone through a learned linear bridge between corresponding source and target feature spaces. We evaluate GRAFT on ten Super-NaturalInstructions text tasks, transferring Qwen2.5 LoRAs to Qwen2.5-VL, and five multimodal tasks, where Qwen2.5-VL LoRAs are directly reused. Compared with randomly initialized LoRA adapters, GRAFT improves performance on most evaluated tasks. These results show that GRAFT provides a simple and effective mechanism for reusing learned capabilities across language and multimodal models in continual learning.

papers.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
papers.summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both the worlds agents interact with and the tasks they must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation. World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components, which are composed into interactive worlds with explicit states, actions, and temporal dynamics. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis, allowing new capabilities to enter evaluation through a shared construction pipeline. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. The stateful design enables task validation and agent evaluation through state correctness and tool-call traces. We evaluate seven models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 68.2% Pass@1. Error analysis reveals challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. Construction experiments demonstrate scalability across domains and token efficiency: world distillation reduces token consumption by 0.9-66.0% and 46.2-92.5% relative to Codex with low and xhigh reasoning effort, respectively, while achieving broader capability coverage. SynthDCB makes executable world construction the basis of scalable device-control benchmarking, connecting an expanding space of capabilities and interactions to verifiable agent evaluation.

papers.title: SERAG: SEmantical and Relational approach for Anomaly detection on knowledge Graphs
papers.summary: Knowledge graphs constructed from text can contain facts that are individually plausible yet inconsistent with their relational context. We introduce SERAG, a supervised anomaly detector that combines two complementary plausibility estimates: a semantic score computed from separately encoded subject, relation, and object labels, and a relational score obtained through a relational graph convolutional network. The scores are standardized, calibrated, and fused. We evaluate the method on a subset of ICEWS18 with vocabulary-constrained synthetic anomalies generated by an LLM, using pooled and chronological splits. At 10% anomaly prevalence, SERAG achieves test AUPRCs of 0.321 and 0.258, respectively, compared with 0.159 and 0.146 for the strongest adapted baseline. Fusion improves mean test AUPRC over either branch alone, with a larger gain in the pooled protocol and a smaller validation-selected gain in the chronological protocol. Additional anomaly supervision improves performance. These results support the complementarity of textual and relational signals for detecting synthetic anomalies under the evaluated protocols.

papers.title: HIMX: mixed-format matrix multiplication based on customized HIFLOAT4 representations
papers.summary: 4-bit weight-activation quantization (W4A4) is an important approach for efficient large language model (LLM) inference. Recent hierarchical formats such as HiFloat4 (HIF4) improve the representational range of 4-bit quantization through multi-level scaling. However, the same local mantissa representation in HIF4 may not be equally suitable for weights and activations, which exhibit distinct distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we propose HiMX, a mixed-mantissa framework built upon the hierarchical scaling structure of HIF4. Our key observation is that the two HIF4-compatible mantissa representations, S1P2 and E2M1, exhibit complementary quantization behavior: the denser S1P2 format provides higher resolution for concentrated weight distributions, while the wider-spaced E2M1 format provides complementary quantization characteristics for activation tensors. HiMX enables operand-tailored mantissa representations while converting heterogeneous mantissas into fixed-point integer operands with operand-specific widths, allowing different operand formats to share a unified integer multiply-accumulate (MAC) array. Block-level analysis on Qwen3-8B shows that HIF4-S1P2 is better suited for weights while HIF4 E2M1 is better suited for activations, and their mixed-format combination achieves lower output MSE than homogeneous configurations. Across multiple benchmarks, HiMX reduces the average end-to-end accuracy loss from 2.38 to 1.77 points on Qwen3-8B and from 2.23 to 1.85 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B, demonstrating the potential benefit of heterogeneous mantissa representations for W4A4 LLM inference.

papers.title: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution
papers.summary: Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and the labeled clinical records needed to train models for them are few, private, and slow to extend, since a specialist must read every case. A model that writes its own training tasks could learn beyond these records, but no program can check a model-written diagnosis, and a wrong answer key corrupts training. To tackle this dilemma between data scarcity and difficulty of data annotations, we introduce RSIMed, Recursive Self-Improvement in Medicine, one of the first self-evolving pipelines in which a task proposer co-evolves in context with a diagnostic solver on real clinical records. Seeded by training admissions, a frozen copy of the solver writes each clinical question from retrieved medical evidence, so its answer rests on a source, and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong. On rare-disease diagnosis from MIMIC-IV admissions, the accuracy of RSIMed-27B grows linearly with training compute, while a static pool of generated tasks collapses. Without any external model, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 diagnostic accuracy, above every off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 setting, whose best reaches 0.399 at 38 times the inference cost of RSIMed-27B. Tasks written by four external teachers, including GPT-5.5, train a less accurate diagnostician than the solver's own. Trained only on diagnosis, RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on the physician-written tasks of HealthBench Professional, from 0.291 to 0.303 in adjusted score.

papers.title: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles
papers.summary: As new models become available, existing ensembles must be updated to be competitive, making them intrinsically dynamic. Deciding whether to add a candidate model can require inference on an entire annotated dataset. Such a screening becomes prohibitive for models with costly inference especially when they ultimately add no value. Even under simple convex aggregation, relying on benchmark scores can be misleading as strong standalone performance does not guarantee ensemble improvement, and fitted ensemble weights can hurt test performance. In this work, we study candidate screening and show how early rejection can be achieved safely, exploiting residual geometry for stratification and rejecting the candidate when the best possible remaining predictions cannot achieve the necessary improvement. The key result that justifies this approach is that, under convex aggregation and squared or Brier loss, the population optimum improves if and only if a candidate induces a prediction change positively aligned with the residuals of the population-optimal existing ensemble. An optimistic quadratic program (QP) provides certified early rejection, while posterior-scenario sampling offers an alternative heuristic. We evaluate the approach by showing the tradeoff between saved calls and screening accuracy, which refers to recovering the same accept/reject result as for the entire annotated dataset. We assess empirically whether full-dataset decisions predict candidate usefulness on a held-out test set. On two LLM panels, stratified screening with certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate calls while keeping 100% screening accuracy. In our experiments, sampling posterior scenarios further increases call savings to approximately 37%, with a loss of less than one percentage point in screening accuracy.

papers.title: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.

papers.title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.

papers.title: Beveridge: Open Weight System One Decision Models with Calibrated Probabilities
papers.summary: Many production systems need a model to make a narrow decision about a document (route a ticket, check a limit, refuse a request, pick the next step of a browser agent) rather than to write text about it. We present Beveridge, a family of open weight System One decision models that take a document and up to 15 typed questions (yes/no, choice among described options, or a level on an ordered scale) and return, in one forward pass without generating text, an answer with a calibrated probability for every option. Beveridge-Large-C (398M parameters) adds a 3.5M parameter decision network to ModernBERT-large: typed number and date features in the input, exact facts from a rule engine, question-to-document evidence attention, a three-step recursive core with learned halting and an exact yes/no path. Beveridge-Pro-C adapts Gemma 4 26B-A4B with LoRA to score option letters, and Beveridge-Pro-C-Web extends it to the next step of a browser agent. On held-out tests the 0.4B model reaches 93.0% on our operations-document benchmark against 91.1% for the best of five general LLMs (31B-675B) and 87.9% for a commercial System One API, and, because its confidences are calibrated (ECE 0.029 on that benchmark), it can hand over 76% of decisions automatically at 95% accuracy, where no general LLM we tested can hand over any. It answers in 4.9 ms per decision on one NVIDIA H200 GPU and 60 ms on the 14 core CPU of an Apple M4 Pro laptop. Beveridge-Pro-C-Web raises next-step accuracy on web pages from unseen site types from 49.4% to 98.2% and completes live browsing tasks without losing document accuracy. We describe the models, the training recipes and an evaluation on 19 held-out test sets against a commercial System One API and five general LLMs, including where the models are weak. Weights and inference code are released under Apache 2.0.

papers.title: Not All Data Leakage Is Equal: A Controlled Benchmark of Evaluation Inflation in Tabular Classification
papers.summary: Data leakage is widely recognized as a threat to trustworthy machine-learning evaluation, yet the phrase covers mechanisms with very different statistical consequences. We present a controlled empirical benchmark that measures the inflation in held-out ROC-AUC caused by five common leakage mechanisms: global standardization, global median imputation, duplicate contamination, supervised feature selection before splitting, and target encoding before splitting. The benchmark spans six public datasets and two synthetic stress tests, three model families, and five repeated stratified train/test splits, yielding 600 paired clean-versus-leaked comparisons. To avoid pseudo-replication, inference is performed on dataset-level effects with cluster bootstrap confidence intervals and Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Label-dependent or direct data-reuse mechanisms produced systematic optimism: global target encoding increased ROC-AUC by 2.42 percentage points on average (95% cluster-bootstrap CI 0.62--4.89), global supervised feature selection by 1.93 points (0.63--3.39), and duplicate contamination by 1.52 points (0.40--2.80). All three remained significant after multiplicity correction. In contrast, global scaling and global median imputation had near-zero average effects under the i.i.d. settings studied here. A controlled target-encoding stress test further shows that leakage becomes sharply worse as categories become sparse. The results support a severity-aware view of leakage: evaluation pipelines should prevent all held-out-data dependence, but label-dependent transformations and observation reuse deserve especially aggressive auditing.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Mambas Selective Gate in Financial Markets: A Leakage-Controlled Study
papers.summary: Selectively gated state-space models (SSMs), notably Mamba, are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes (bull, bear, sideways) remains opaque. This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) to a six-layer Mamba trained on approximately twenty-one years of daily data for a point-in-time set of S&P 500 constituents plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decomposing per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our central contribution is methodological and cautionary. A prior, uncontrolled configuration recovered market regimes from SAE features at F1 = 1.00. Under a controlled protocol that (i) removes the three input features that overlap the HMM label definition, (ii) disables the auxiliary regime-classification head, (iii) uses a point-in-time constituent universe, and (iv) evaluates against labels disjoint from the inputs, the same regime label is recovered at only F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and from an SAE trained on a randomly initialized, untrained Mamba (0.364). A 2x2 attribution grid shows the near-perfect result is an interaction of auxiliary supervision and label-defining inputs: neither factor alone exceeds F1 ~ 0.40. Effect sizes with block-bootstrap inference show the residual selective-gate (Delta t) regime effect is statistically detectable but economically negligible and uniform across layers rather than layer-specialized; the apparent polysemanticity gradient disappears under continuous, theory-grounded measures. We contribute a reproducible leakage-control protocol for interpretability evaluation of financial SSMs, a quantified demonstration that previously reported regime structure is a label-contamination artifact, and a modest economically grounded feature subset that genuinely survives the controls.

papers.title: Ensemble Bounds for Pairwise Dissimilar Decomposition of Deterministic Datasets
papers.summary: In this paper, we study reduced similarity decompositions of \emph{deterministic} datasets using redundancy graphs and obtain \emph{ensemble} bounds for the minimum size of such constrained decomposition. We consider batch decompositions that reduce similarity \emph{across} batches and use the Lov\'asz local lemma to obtain bounds for the minimum size of a decomposition with a given pairwise dissimilarity. We then consider unique batch decomposition with a given relaxation parameter and obtain upper and lower ensemble bounds for the minimum size. Throughout, we use Binomial random graphs to obtain the desired ensemble bounds, by conditioning on the number of similar \emph{pairs} of data points.

papers.title: Multimodal Fusion with Pre-trained Models for Psychotherapy Outcome Prediction from Emotional Dynamics
papers.summary: In-session emotional dynamics are associated with psychotherapy outcomes but difficult to measure at scale. Pretrained multimodal models provide automated access to facial, vocal, and textual signals, yet clinical datasets remain small. Our research question is how pretrained multimodal representations can best support psychotherapy outcome prediction under data scarcity. Three studies use 106 sessions from 88 patients and nine session-level outcome scales (HSCL-11, EPO-1, POMS). Study 1 asks whether deep learning outperforms classical machine learning: a two-stage deep pipeline, first predicting window-level valence/arousal and then session outcomes, transferred poorly (best single configuration, $r=.078$). Study 2 asks which representation and preprocessing choices work best: statistical pooling of frozen pretrained embeddings with regularized classical models achieved average $r=.406$ across nine scales under per-scale configuration selection, up to $r=.490$ for symptom distress, with complementary modalities and no significant benefit from manual affect annotations or therapist features. Study 3 asks whether deep learning remains inferior under these choices: classical models outperformed an optimized single-stage deep model at the single-configuration level ($r=.281$ vs. $.222$) and on all nine scales under matched per-scale selection ($.406$ vs. $.252$). The results suggest that under clinical data scarcity, pretrained representations with fixed statistical pooling and regularized classical models are more reliable than learned aggregation.

papers.title: Predictive maintenance in manufacturing: The operational value of continual machine learning
papers.summary: Predictive maintenance in high-volume manufacturing often faces a domain-incremental learning problem: as new product configurations enter production, prediction models must learn from newly available data while preserving performance on earlier configurations that remain in operation. In this paper, we empirically study the operational value of continual machine learning methods for addressing this challenge in predictive maintenance, using real-world maintenance data from Bosch. The setting at Bosch covers 25 product configurations over five years, which creates a practical challenge for predictive maintenance models, as such models must be updated with data from newly introduced configurations without reducing performance on configurations learned earlier, a phenomenon known as "forgetting". At the same time, retaining all historical sensor data and repeatedly retraining models is often infeasible in high-volume manufacturing since industrial machines generate too large data volumes. To address this challenge, we combine continual machine learning with robust optimization to support predictive maintenance. We then compare continual machine learning with a broad set of baselines, including fine-tuning, domain-adaptation methods, online learning methods, and configuration-specific models. Across experiments, continual machine learning methods achieve stronger predictive performance and lower maintenance costs than the baselines, with a reduction of cost-related indicators of more than 40 % relative to the baselines. Our results demonstrate the operational value of continual machine learning for decision support in maintenance when product portfolios grow over time and historical manufacturing data cannot be fully retained.

papers.title: Agents Cannot Hand Over What They Have Not Yet Understood
papers.summary: Agents that work beyond a single context window, or in teams, hand their work to a successor as a short written summary. Evaluation has focused on whether an agent can solve a task, and relatively little is known about how much of what an agent has learned survives being written down. We study this in 56 interactive worlds with hidden rules, where an agent that is told nothing fails and an agent given a 300-character statement of the rules succeeds. We compare one agent that plays eight lives and keeps its whole history with a chain of eight agents that each play one life and inherit a 300-character note. All six models we test learn less in the chain: after eight generations it stands where the single agent stood after about four lives. Controlled variants of the chain decompose this handoff loss into three components: none from changing the agent, a smaller loss from compressing to 300 characters, and a larger loss from compressing repeatedly. When each note is written from the full record of earlier lives instead of from the previous note, the same 300 characters recover 70% to 82% of the loss. The loss is robust across model sizes and is not alleviated by instructing the writer to record evidence, to revise the inherited note, or to keep a structured ledger. In simpler terms, an agent cannot hand over what it has not yet understood: a note holds what its writer has worked out, and a rule that takes several lives to see is lost with the lives that were not passed on.

papers.title: FedFit: Federated Dynamic Sparse Training via Fisher Information scoring
papers.summary: Cross-device Federated Learning (FL) is frequently bottlenecked by the prohibitive memory and communication costs of training deep neural networks on resource-constrained edge hardware. While federated dynamic sparse training aims to alleviate these costs by adjusting sparse structures during training, existing methods rely on magnitude-based heuristics that are fundamentally ill-suited for the non-convergent, heterogeneous environments inherent to FL. To address this challenge, we propose FedFit, a federated dynamic sparse training framework that replaces simple heuristics with optimization-centric criteria for structure adjustment. By leveraging a second-order approximation of the loss landscape via the Fisher Information Matrix, FedFit enables precise and efficient structure adjustment without the overhead of explicit Hessian computation. Empirical evaluations across computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks demonstrate that FedFit significantly narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high communication efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/Serena-28/Fedfit.git .

papers.title: Minari: Infrastructure for Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Datasets
papers.summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) depends on shared datasets, but sharing them is still hard. Each benchmark ships its own format, documentation is thin, and most datasets cannot be regenerated once the environment code moves on. We introduce Minari, an open-source Python library for creating, sharing, and loading RL datasets. Its API follows Gymnasium, so recording a dataset means wrapping an environment and stepping through it as usual. From there, users can attach metadata, filter, combine, and shuffle datasets, and publish or download them with one command through the HuggingFace Hub. Every dataset stores the environment specification, seeds, applied wrappers, and pinned package requirements needed to rebuild the environment and regenerate the data. TorchRL, AgileRL, and d3rlpy already load Minari datasets natively, so switching datasets in those libraries takes one line of code. Minari also hosts 338 reproducible datasets (350K trajectories, 55M steps) covering robotic locomotion and manipulation, maze and grid navigation, language-conditioned instruction following, Atari, and web navigation, including a full regeneration of D4RL with public generation scripts. We report baseline scores for six offline RL algorithms on the regenerated D4RL and MuJoCo datasets.

papers.title: Domino: Joint Unmasking via First-order Markov Chain for Few-Step Masked Diffusion
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models generate a sequence by revealing masked positions over many denoising steps. A few-step sampler has to reveal many positions at once, but the standard reverse kernel draws them independently and primarily ignores the conditional dependence between tokens revealed in the same step. We propose a novel framework called Domino, which models this dependence with a first-order Markov chain over the revealed positions, given the current state. The first revealed position keeps the posterior of a pre-trained masked diffusion model (MDM), and each subsequent position follows a transition given the token of its predecessor. Notably, the resulting step is normalized by construction, contains the factorized step in MDMs as a special case, and has a likelihood in closed form. We implement the Domino transitions via a lightweight module on the hidden states of a pre-trained MDM denoiser with only 2.6% parameter overhead and train by keeping the MDM denoiser frozen. Our extensive evaluations across text, molecules, and images show that Domino lowers the few-step generative perplexity of MDMs by a factor of 1.7 to 3.8 on One Billion Word (LM1B), WikiText-103, and OpenWebText at nearly unchanged sample entropy. It also raises the validity of few-step molecule samples by 1.5x. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/domino.git

papers.title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
papers.summary: We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design variables.We focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic specification.We instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional routing.This turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

papers.title: Earth World Model: Physics-constrained latent dynamics for forecasting and environmental scenario analysis
papers.summary: World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.

papers.title: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
papers.summary: Sparse and delayed rewards make reinforcement learning challenging for long-horizon language agents. On-policy distillation (OPD) complements environmental rewards with dense teacher feedback on student-generated contexts. Standard OPD can misalign supervision with relative teacher competence, student trajectory outcomes, and the temporal structure of task execution. Recent variants adjust guidance through divergence-based weighting and temporal schedules, while joint calibration from task-completion experience remains underexplored. We introduce Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (ECOD), which allocates teacher supervision at the task, trajectory, and turn levels. ECOD compares teacher and student success-rate posteriors under matched task conditions, restricts direct supervision to failed student trajectories, and derives a temporal prior from successful teacher lengths. The resulting weight applies to teacher losses or teacher-derived advantages. We evaluate ECOD on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Under matched teacher settings, ECOD improves standard OPD by up to 4.06% in relative ALFWorld unseen success. Across both model scales, ECOD-assisted SOD, TCOD-F2B, and ATOD configurations yield average paired relative gains of 6.20% on ALFWorld unseen and 7.05% on WebShop, with WebShop gains ranging from 2.29% to 21.60%. These results support experience-calibrated supervision allocation as a reusable mechanism across distinct distillation objectives.

papers.title: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification
papers.summary: Complete formal verification of neural networks is crucial for their deployment in safety-critical domains. A key bottleneck stems from encoding complexity: traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron. We propose the Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART), which fundamentally breaks the conventional one-to-one mapping between unstable neurons and binary variables by establishing formal reducibility criteria. This allows for finer-grained modeling, where each unstable neuron corresponds on average to fewer than one binary variable, thereby reducing verification complexity at its source. Based on SART, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the number of binary variables required for complete verification and, under the assumption that $P \neq NP$, prove that variables in the final layer can be compressed by 50\%, while the number of variables in intermediate layers cannot be further reduced. To overcome the apparent ``last-layer-only'' limitation, we recast verification as a sequential process and, crucially, show that the gain lifts to the entire network: LayerABS, a SART-based progressive tightening verifier, iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers and propagates tight bounds that shrink the global search space and binary-variable counts. Furthermore, we reveal a structural law influencing verification complexity: when the signs of weights of unstable neurons satisfy numerical symmetry, with positive and negative weights equal or differing by at most one, the worst-case verification complexity achieves the theoretical optimum, offering theoretical guidance for the design of verification-friendly architectures. As a general-purpose underlying encoding, the value of SART is independent of specific algorithms.

papers.title: Rethinking the Verification of Machine Unlearning
papers.summary: Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.

papers.title: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
papers.summary: Stagewise algorithms and sparsity-inducing regularization are two influential approaches to high-dimensional modeling. Existing stagewise theory, however, largely centers on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and other structural preferences are often pursued through fixed-level nonconvex optimization rather than generating an entire adaptive solution path. We develop stagewise adaptive boosting, a general framework that builds a monotone path by selecting the update consistent with structural preference. The framework can encourage sparsity along the path itself and also admits extensions that promote other properties of the solution, including group selection, similarity across models for multiple outcomes, and known priorities or prerequisite relations among predictors. We study its theoretical property as well as finite sample performance using simulations and real-data analyses. Across these studies, the proposed pathwise approach often achieves predictive performance comparable to commonly used baselines while selecting substantially smaller models. These results suggest that adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical route to stronger sparsity and richer structural control without repeatedly solving separate weighted or nonconvex optimization problems.

papers.title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
papers.summary: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.

papers.title: Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks: Constrained Deep Learning for Sex-Specific Multi-Population Longevity Forecasting
papers.summary: We introduce Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained deep learning framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that embeds actuarial knowledge into LSTM training through differentiable penalty terms. Applied to a high-longevity 6-country cluster (Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, West Germany, Netherlands, Japan; 1956-2020), the framework is a challenger to the Li-Lee benchmark and unconstrained neural approaches. Our central finding is that monotonicity constraint intensity lambda functions as a continuous governance dial with a quantifiable accuracy-stability trade-off. At lambda = 0.01, 30-year forecast confidence intervals narrow by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost. At lambda = 0.1, they narrow by 25% at only +0.84% RMSE cost. This trade-off is invisible to standard hyperparameter optimizers, which select lambda by minimizing one-step RMSE, the wrong metric for structural constraints in recursive forecasting. The framework adds three contributions: (i) residual-calibrated process noise that eliminates double-counting in the dual uncertainty framework, reducing confidence intervals by 53-60%; (ii) a 5-seed model ensemble with a coefficient of variation of 1.06%; and (iii) a time-varying credibility weight Z(t) = exp(-alpha t) connecting to Buhlmann credibility theory for blending neural and actuarial predictions. A 10-year out-of-sample backtest (trained on 1956-2010, validated against observed HMD life expectancy for 2011-2020) yields a mean absolute error of 0.38 years, with 11 of 12 country x sex combinations within the 90% confidence interval. The model produces regulatory-grade outputs including Solvency Capital Requirements under the Swiss Solvency Test (ES 99.0%: +1.91 years, CHE Male) and Solvency II, reverse stress testing, and model-based stability verification (amplification ratio 1.02x).

papers.title: Recovered or Memorized? Investigating Dynamical Consistency and Faithfulness in World Model Latents
papers.summary: World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fr\'echet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.

papers.title: Trajectory-Based Bayesian Discovery of a Host-Pathogen Model from Quasi-Steady-State Observations
papers.summary: System identification of nonlinear dynamical systems becomes challenging when the measured data come from a nearly settled state. We study this situation in the case of a bistable host-pathogen interaction model with a cubic term, whose seven true mechanisms are hidden among twenty candidate terms. The data are from one noise-free trajectory on a quasi-steady-state observed window and the initial state. In this situation, classical sparse identification approaches fail to identify the correct mechanisms as the candidate library becomes ill-conditioned along the quasi-steady-state trajectory. To address this, we propose an alternative approach in which sparse Bayesian learning and $\ell_{0}$ iterative hard thresholding with pursuit provide a good start, and a two-swap climb on the Bayesian evidence of the candidate ODE solutions recovers the true model. Our results show successful model recovery, i.e., correct identification of its support and accurate estimation of its coefficients, as validated by exhaustive scoring.

papers.title: What explainable deep learning reveals about wall-bounded turbulence: insights from conditional surprisal
papers.summary: Explainable deep learning (XDL) has identified regions of wall turbulence important for prediction that are only partly captured by classical coherent-structure criteria. We examine turbulent channel flow at friction Reynolds numbers $Re_\tau\simeq125$ and $550$ by comparing SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with conditional surprisal, which quantifies how unexpected an observed velocity transition is given its initial state. Although SHAP selection favours energetic fluid and largely overlaps classical masks, selected fluid outside these masks is less energetic but exhibits higher surprisal. Near the wall, at comparable fluctuation energy and wall distance, high-surprisal voxels outside classical masks are approximately 11 and 5 times more likely to be selected by SHAP than low-surprisal voxels, respectively. Within classical masks, the factor is about 1.3. SHAP-selected structures containing paired high- and low-speed regions exhibit surprisal maxima near their internal $u=0$ interfaces, where transverse velocity fluctuations remain nonzero. These interfaces contain vortical and SHAP-only regions, with the latter accounting for more than half of their reconstructed area. In part of the buffer layer, the SHAP-only portions have higher mean surprisal than the vortical portions. However, comparison with generic $u=0$ surfaces indicates that much of the raw interfacial surprisal excess is associated with surrounding fluctuation energy; after energy matching, the equally weighted surface comparison is statistically compatible with unity on the retained common support. Together, these results show how state-conditioned velocity transitions complement instantaneous structure-identification criteria in characterizing SHAP-selected flow.
